history.content: My maize keeps getting shorter and the yield drops a little more each season, and the bottom leaves are pale. What steps should I take?

draws.answer: Those signs are typical of nitrogen depletion in your maize. Start by inspecting the leaves; the uniform pale yellow on older lower leaves indicates nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. Then, return organic matter to the soil by applying manure, compost, or by burying residues instead of burning them, because mineral fertilizer alone does not work on exhausted soil. After that, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the appropriate fertilizer dose for your plot. I cannot give you a precise fertilizer rate without that analysis.

history.content: My tomato garden has a lot of weeds and the leaves look a bit sick, how can I find out if whiteflies or aphids are the cause?

draws.answer: You need to examine the underside of your tomato leaves to tell the pest apart. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on several plants; if you see many tiny insects that stay in packed colonies on the leaf undersides, whiteflies are likely. Then give the leaves a shake to look closely. If you see a sticky film and a cloud of tiny white insects flying up and settling back down, aphids are the cause. Remove the most heavily infested leaves and destroy them, and clear weeds around the plot edges. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies, and use a strong spray of water to dislodge aphids while the insects are off the plant. For the approved product and its rate, see ICAT.

The catalogue says the reverse: replanting the trees is the first aim in time, and the crops are practised secondarily, for a limited period of two to three years, so as to let the trees grow well. It is a technique for places where land pressure is strong. That is why the crop sequence is fixed and short: cowpea, groundnut or pea the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize the two following years. After those two or three years the cropping stops. history.content: True or false: in the Taungya method the crop is the main aim and the trees are just there to help it.

draws.answer: False. The catalogue's first aim is that the crops be grown underneath the trees for only two or three years, so the trees can grow tall enough to carry the crop. Then in the three years after that the cropping continues, with the trees leaving the soil as organic fertiliser and keeping birds, insects and small animals at the same time. The crops are an accompaniment, not the crop.

False. The method is the opposite: the trees are chosen and planted first, then the fields are left fallow for two or three years, at which point the trees are pruned and the crops planted in their place. So the trees are the main aim at the start, not the crops afterwards. The trees are also the one part of the practice people forget when they see them: they are pruned in such a way that a high cut is left at the base, which the catalogue describes as leaving a firebreak into the field.

Go through the herd and pull the ticks from the ears, under the tail and between the legs. After you have removed the ticks, call the veterinary service the same day so they can tell you which disease it is and give the correct drug and dose. Then, if it is Kara or Savanes, use the single-season plan; if Maritime or Plateaux, use the double-season plan; if Centrale, expect a mixed pattern. After you state the region, contact ICAT for the prefecture-level calendar that gives the exact planting dates.

history.content: I'm unsure if my village follows the north or south planting pattern. How can I find out?

draws.answer: You need to know which of the five regions your village falls under: Kara or Savanes is northern, Maritime or Plateaux is southern, and Centrale is a middle zone. The north has one rainy season, so you sow at the start of the reliable rains, not after a single shower. The south has two rainy seasons, so sow when the rains are properly established, not at the first shower. Centrale shows a transitional pattern between the two. For exact calendars for your prefecture, ask ICAT.

The north and south patterns are defined by the five regions: Maritime, Plateaux, Centrale, Kara, and Savanes. Kara and Savanes are north areas, so you plant there. Maritime and Plateaux are south areas, so you plant there. Centrale is a transition zone, so you can sow anywhere within it. Ask an extension officer to tell you your exact region. If you need help turning this into a calendar, contact ICAT.
